title: Acceleration: how velocity changes every second
summary: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity—not how fast you move, and negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down. Master signs, braking steps, and the v–t graph.

u.label: $u$
u.body: The train's starting velocity along $+x$ at $t = 0$.

vel.label: $v$
vel.meaning: velocity after 6 s of braking: +6 m/s (east)
vel.body: Still positive, so the train is still moving east—just much slower than before.

time.label: $t$
time.body: The time over which velocity changes from [u:$u$] to [vel:$v$].

dv.label: $\Delta v$
dv.body: Always **final minus initial**: $v - u = 6 - 24 = -18\text{ m/s}$. The minus sign shows the velocity shifted westward.

accel.label: $a$
accel.body: Defined by {accel_card|acceleration}: $\Delta v / t$. Here $a = -3\text{ m/s}^2$, meaning velocity drops by $3\text{ m/s}$ every second.
accel.example: $-3\text{ m/s}^2$ directed west while moving east means braking.
accel.analogy: How fast the speedometer needle sweeps downward each second while braking.

disp.label: $s$
disp.meaning: displacement covered during the 6 s braking interval, in meters
disp.body: Found from {mean_speed|the mean speed theorem} or {suvat|uniform acceleration equations}, and equal to the signed area under the {vt_graph|$v\text{–}t$ graph}.

t_stop.label: $t_{\text{stop}}$
t_stop.meaning: extra time needed to slow from 6 m/s to 0 m/s
t_stop.body: How many more seconds at $a = -3\text{ m/s}^2$ erase the remaining $6\text{ m/s}$ of velocity.

sign_of_a.title: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down
sign_of_a.body: The sign of [accel:$a$] only tells you the **direction** of the acceleration vector ($+x$ or $-x$). An object **speeds up** when $v$ and $a$ have the **same sign** (both $+$ or both $-$), and **slows down** (decelerates) when $v$ and $a$ have **opposite signs**.
sign_of_a.example: Moving west at $v = -10\text{ m/s}$ with $a = -2\text{ m/s}^2$ reaches $-12\text{ m/s}$ after $1\text{ s}$—it got faster!
sign_of_a.useWhen: a problem gives a negative acceleration and asks whether the object speeds up or slows down.

vt_graph.title: Reading a velocity–time ($v\text{–}t$) graph
vt_graph.body: On a $v\text{–}t$ graph, the **slope** equals [accel:acceleration] $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$, and the **signed area** between the curve and the time axis equals [disp:displacement] $s$. A straight tilted line means constant acceleration.
vt_graph.example: A trapezoid from $u = 24\text{ m/s}$ to $v = 6\text{ m/s}$ over $6\text{ s}$ has area $\frac{24+6}{2} \times 6 = 90\text{ m}$.
vt_graph.useWhen: you are given a velocity–time graph or want to check a kinematic formula visually.

sections.title: Velocity changes, not velocity itself
sections.body: A jet cruising smoothly at $250\text{ m/s}$ in a straight line has **zero** acceleration, whereas a car just starting to roll from rest has a large acceleration. {accel_card|Acceleration} is a vector measuring how much {speed_vel|velocity} changes each second—whether it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. In 1D motion, watching the signs of both $v$ and $a$ prevents the classic trap in {sign_of_a|negative acceleration}.

sections.title: How the signs of velocity and acceleration work together
sections.note: compare the sign of $v$ with the sign of $a$ every time

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
A commuter train travels straight east ($+x$) at initial velocity [u:$u = 24\text{ m/s}$]. The driver brakes steadily for [time:$t = 6\text{ s}$], reducing the train's velocity to [vel:$v = 6\text{ m/s}$] east.

Find (1) the constant [accel:acceleration] $a$, (2) the [disp:displacement] $s$ during these $6\text{ s}$, and (3) the [t_stop:additional time] needed at the same acceleration to come to a complete stop ($v = 0$).

sections.title: Identify the five kinematic quantities
sections.note: take east as the positive $+x$ axis

rows.note: final velocity after $6\text{ s}$, still eastward

sections.title: Concept → Field
sections.concept: When [accel:acceleration] is constant, velocity changes linearly ($v = u + at$) and {dist_disp|displacement} equals average velocity times time, $s = \dfrac{u+v}{2}\,t$.
sections.field: Kinematics (uniformly accelerated 1D motion). Built from {accel_card|acceleration}, {mean_speed|the mean speed theorem}, and {suvat|uniform acceleration equations}.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: order the steps so each one uses only values you already know

routes.title: Route A
routes.why: Definition of acceleration gives $a$ directly; {mean_speed|the mean speed theorem} finds $s$ without even needing $a$; then $v = u + at$ finishes the stop time.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. Every step is short and self-checking.

routes.title: Route B
routes.why: Subtracting the smaller number from the bigger number avoids a minus sign.
routes.whyNot: Reversing $v - u$ flips the sign of [accel:$a$]. Writing $+3\text{ m/s}^2$ claims the train accelerated **eastward** to $42\text{ m/s}$ instead of braking!

sections.notUsed: Not used: the train's mass. Kinematics describes how velocity and position evolve without needing forces.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover a step to trace every symbol and sign

steps.move: Find the change in velocity [dv:$\Delta v$] (final minus initial).
steps.why: A change is always final minus initial. The negative result means the velocity decreased by $18\text{ m/s}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not compute $24 - 6 = +18$: that flips the direction of change.

steps.move: Divide [dv:$\Delta v$] by [time:$t$] to get constant [accel:acceleration].
steps.why: By {accel_card|acceleration}, the train's velocity shifts by $-3\text{ m/s}$ ($3\text{ m/s}$ west) each second. Since $v > 0$ and $a < 0$, {sign_of_a|the train slows down}.
steps.whyNot: Do not confuse $-3\text{ m/s}^2$ with a velocity: the train is still moving east at $+6\text{ m/s}$, not backward.

steps.move: Compute [disp:displacement] during the $6\text{ s}$ braking period using {mean_speed|average velocity}.
steps.why: With constant acceleration, average velocity is halfway between $u$ and $v$ ($15\text{ m/s}$), matching the trapezoid area on the {vt_graph|$v\text{–}t$ graph}. Cross-check via {suvat|$ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$}: $24(6) + \frac{1}{2}(-3)(6^2) = 144 - 54 = 90\text{ m}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not plug $+3$ into $ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$: forgetting the minus sign gives $144 + 54 = 198\text{ m}$, larger than even $24 \times 6 = 144\text{ m}$!

steps.move: Find the [t_stop:extra time] to drop from [vel:$6\text{ m/s}$] to $0\text{ m/s}$ at [accel:$a = -3\text{ m/s}^2$].
steps.why: Losing $3\text{ m/s}$ every second erases the remaining $6\text{ m/s}$ in exactly $2\text{ s}$ (total braking time from $24\text{ m/s}$ to rest is $6 + 2 = 8\text{ s}$).
steps.whyNot: Do not answer $8\text{ s}$ when the question asks for the *additional* time after the first $6\text{ s}$.

sections.title: Velocity–time ($v\text{–}t$) graph: slope is acceleration
sections.note: drag initial velocity $u$, acceleration $a$, and time $t$; notice what happens after the line crosses $v = 0$

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Bounds on displacement**: at $u = 24\text{ m/s}$ and $v = 6\text{ m/s}$ over $6\text{ s}$, $s$ must sit between $6 \times 6 = 36\text{ m}$ and $24 \times 6 = 144\text{ m}$—and $90\text{ m}$ is right in the middle.
**Cross-check with $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$**: $6^2 = 36$ and $24^2 + 2(-3)(90) = 576 - 540 = 36$. Every {suvat|kinematic equation} agrees.

**Watch the zero crossing**: drag $t$ from $6\text{ s}$ to $8\text{ s}$ ($v = 0$, $s = 96\text{ m}$), then to $10\text{ s}$ ($v = -6\text{ m/s}$)—beyond $8\text{ s}$, $v$ and $a$ are both negative, so the object **speeds up** in the $-x$ direction.
**Zero velocity $\neq$ zero acceleration**: at the exact instant $t = 8\text{ s}$ when $v = 0$, the slope of the $v\text{–}t$ line is still $-3\text{ m/s}^2$, not zero.

questions.q: A motorbike speeds up uniformly in a straight line from $8\text{ m/s}$ to $28\text{ m/s}$ in $5\text{ s}$. What is its acceleration?
A car moves along the $-x$ axis with velocity $v = -12\text{ m/s}$ and constant acceleration $a = -2\text{ m/s}^2$. What happens to its speed?
options: It slows down because $a$ is negative
It keeps a constant speed of $12\text{ m/s}$
It speeds up in the $-x$ direction because $v$ and $a$ have the same sign
questions.why: By {sign_of_a|sign comparison}, after $1\text{ s}$ the velocity becomes $-14\text{ m/s}$ (speed rises from $12$ to $14\text{ m/s}$).

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight upward. At its highest point, its instantaneous velocity is $0\text{ m/s}$. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration at that instant?
questions.why: Gravity never turns off at the peak: velocity passes smoothly from positive through zero to negative, so the slope $a = g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ downward stays constant.

questions.q: On a velocity–time ($v\text{–}t$) graph, what do the **slope** and the **signed area** between the curve and the time axis represent?
questions.why: On a {vt_graph|$v\text{–}t$ graph}, $\Delta v / \Delta t$ (slope) is acceleration, while multiplying velocity by time (area) gives displacement.
